---
title: "Replicating Hamerly and Elkan (2003)"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
options(digits = 4L)
```

[Hamerly and Elkan (2003)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2003/file/234833147b97bb6aed53a8f4f1c7a7d8-Paper.pdf)
evaluate G-means on synthetic data (their Table 1), study the statistical power of the split test
(their Figure 3), and cluster two real datasets of handwritten digits. This article reruns these
experiments with `gmeans()`. The paper also compares G-means with X-means and the BIC and reports
run times, which are left out here.

The defaults of `gmeans()` follow the paper: the search starts from one center (`k_init = 1`), the
Anderson-Darling test uses the significance level `level = 0.0001`, and the number of clusters is
not capped (`k_max = Inf`). The paper provides neither its data nor its code, so the synthetic data
below are regenerated from its description, and the results can only be compared approximately.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(gmeans)
```

## Synthetic data

Each synthetic dataset in the paper has 5000 points in \(d = 2\), 8, or 32 dimensions, drawn from
\(k = 5\), 20, or 80 Gaussian clusters. The cluster means are uniform in the unit hypercube, and
\(\sigma\) is chosen so that no two means are closer than \(3\sigma\). Each cluster is made
non-spherical by a random scaling and rotation matrix. The paper does not say how the scaling is
drawn, so here each dimension is scaled by a factor drawn uniformly between 0.2 and 1, which keeps
every cluster at most \(\sigma\) wide in any direction.

```{r}
simulate_clusters <- function(k, d, n = 5000L) {
  centers <- matrix(runif(k * d), nrow = k)
  sigma <- min(dist(centers)) / 3
  cluster <- rep_len(seq_len(k), n)
  x <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = d)
  for (j in seq_len(k)) {
    rows <- which(cluster == j)
    rotation <- qr.Q(qr(matrix(rnorm(d * d), nrow = d)))
    shape <- diag(runif(d, 0.2, 1), nrow = d) %*% rotation
    noise <- matrix(rnorm(length(rows) * d), ncol = d)
    x[rows, ] <- sweep(sigma * noise %*% shape, 2L, centers[j, ], "+")
  }
  list(x = x, cluster = cluster)
}
```

The paper reports the number of clusters found and the distortion relative to the distortion of the
true clustering, both as mean and standard deviation over 30 datasets per setting. Splitting the
data into more clusters than there are lowers the distortion below 1, and so does k-means moving
points near the boundary between two clusters to the closer center. A distortion above 1 means the
clusters found fit the data worse than the true clusters.

```{r}
optimal_distortion <- function(x, cluster) {
  sum(vapply(
    split(seq_len(nrow(x)), cluster),
    \(rows) sum(scale(x[rows, , drop = FALSE], scale = FALSE)^2),
    numeric(1L)
  ))
}

set.seed(2003)
settings <- CJ(d = c(2L, 8L, 32L), k = c(5L, 20L, 80L), rep = 1:30)
synthetic <- settings[,
  {
    sim <- simulate_clusters(k, d)
    fit <- gmeans(sim$x)
    .(
      k_found = nrow(fit$centers),
      distortion = fit$tot.withinss / optimal_distortion(sim$x, sim$cluster)
    )
  },
  by = .(d, k, rep)
]
```

```{r}
mean_sd <- function(x, digits) {
  sprintf("%.*f ± %.*f", digits, mean(x), digits, sd(x))
}

replicated <- synthetic[,
  .(k_found = mean_sd(k_found, 1L), distortion = mean_sd(distortion, 2L)),
  by = .(d, k)
]

paper <- rowwiseDT(
  d = , k = , paper_k_found = , paper_distortion = ,
   2L ,  5L , "9.1 ± 9.9"     , "0.89 ± 0.23"      ,
   2L , 20L , "20.1 ± 0.6"    , "0.99 ± 0.01"      ,
   2L , 80L , "80.0 ± 0.2"    , "1.00 ± 0.01"      ,
   8L ,  5L , "5.0 ± 0.0"     , "1.00 ± 0.00"      ,
   8L , 20L , "20.0 ± 0.1"    , "0.99 ± 0.00"      ,
   8L , 80L , "80.2 ± 0.5"    , "0.99 ± 0.00"      ,
  32L ,  5L , "5.0 ± 0.0"     , "1.00 ± 0.00"      ,
  32L , 20L , "20.0 ± 0.0"    , "1.00 ± 0.00"      ,
  32L , 80L , "80.0 ± 0.0"    , "1.00 ± 0.00"
)

comparison <- paper[replicated, on = .(d, k)]
knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  col.names = c("d", "true k", "k found (paper)", "distortion (paper)", "k found", "distortion"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

In most settings `gmeans()` finds about the true number of clusters, as in the paper. With five
clusters in two dimensions, both the paper and `gmeans()` sometimes split the non-spherical clusters
into many pieces. Since the scaling of the clusters is not specified in the paper, the datasets here
are not the same as in the paper, so the results can differ by more than chance.

With 80 clusters in 32 dimensions, `gmeans()` usually finds a few clusters too many (median
`r median(synthetic[d == 32L & k == 80L, k_found])`), while the paper finds
exactly 80. Each cluster here has only about 62 points. With so few points in so many dimensions,
the two-center k-means of the split test can find a direction along which even a single Gaussian
cluster looks like two, so the test splits Gaussian clusters more often than the level of 0.0001
suggests. With 80 clusters tested in every round, a few such splits add up.

```{r}
stopped_early <- synthetic[k_found < k / 2]
stopped_early
```

In `r nrow(stopped_early)` of the `r nrow(synthetic)` datasets, `gmeans()` stops with less than half
of the true clusters. This is a limitation of G-means itself: when a split does not separate the
clusters cleanly, each part still contains many clusters, and projected onto the split direction
such a mixture can look Gaussian enough to pass the test at the strict level of 0.0001.

## Statistical power

Figure 3 of the paper shows how often the split test makes the wrong decision, as a function of the
number of points \(n\). A type I error splits one Gaussian cluster, here with one axis 5% shorter
than the other. A type II error does not split two Gaussian clusters whose means are \(5\sigma\)
apart. The paper runs 1000 tests per point.

```{r}
set.seed(2003)
error_rates <- data.table(n = c(10L, 20L, 30L, 50L, 100L, 150L, 200L))
error_rates <- error_rates[,
  {
    type_1 <- replicate(1000L, {
      x <- matrix(rnorm(2L * n), ncol = 2L) %*% diag(c(1, 0.95))
      nrow(gmeans(x)$centers) > 1L
    })
    type_2 <- replicate(1000L, {
      x <- matrix(rnorm(2L * n), ncol = 2L)
      x[seq_len(n %/% 2L), 1L] <- x[seq_len(n %/% 2L), 1L] + 5
      nrow(gmeans(x)$centers) == 1L
    })
    .(
      error = c("Type I: splits one cluster", "Type II: does not split two clusters"),
      rate = c(mean(type_1), mean(type_2))
    )
  },
  by = n
]
```

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5, dpi = 300}
ggplot(error_rates, aes(n, rate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~error) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Number of points", y = "Error rate")
```

As in the paper, the test almost never splits a single Gaussian cluster, while it needs enough
points to split two clusters. In the paper the type II error is close to 1 at 10 and 20 points,
about 0.37 at 50 points, and 0 from 100 points on. Here it is
`r error_rates[n == 30L & startsWith(error, "Type II"), rate]` at 30
points, `r error_rates[n == 50L & startsWith(error, "Type II"), rate]` at 50
points, and `r error_rates[n == 100L & startsWith(error, "Type II"), rate]`
at 100 points. A larger `level`
trades a higher type I error for more power on small clusters.

## Handwritten digits

The paper clusters the Pendigits dataset from the
[UCI repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/81/pen+based+recognition+of+handwritten+digits),
16 features of pen trajectories of the digits 0 to 9, and reports 69 clusters with a partition
quality of 0.196. The partition quality compares the clusters \(j\) with the true classes \(i\):
\[
  \mathrm{PQ} = \frac{\sum_{i} \sum_{j} p(i, j)^2}{\sum_{i} p(i)^2},
\]
where \(p(i, j)\) is the share of points in class \(i\) and cluster \(j\), and \(p(i)\) is the
share of points in class \(i\). It is 1 whenever each class lies within a single cluster, and it
decreases as the classes are split into more clusters. It does not penalize merging classes: putting
all points into one cluster also gives 1.

The paper describes the data as 7984 examples, which matches neither the training set (7494
examples) nor the full dataset (10992 examples) on UCI. The training set is used here, since it is
the closest. The file `pendigits-train.csv` next to this article is a copy of `pendigits.tra`, the
training set by Alpaydin and Alimoglu (1996),
[doi:10.24432/C5MG6K](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5MG6K), licensed under
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

```{r}
pendigits <- fread(
  "pendigits-train.csv",
  header = FALSE,
  col.names = c(paste0("x", 1:16), "digit")
)
x <- as.matrix(pendigits[, !"digit"])
digit <- pendigits$digit

partition_quality <- function(truth, cluster) {
  p <- table(truth, cluster) / length(truth)
  sum(p^2) / sum(rowSums(p)^2)
}

fit <- gmeans(x)
nrow(fit$centers)
partition_quality(digit, fit$cluster)
```

`gmeans()` finds `r nrow(fit$centers)` clusters with a partition quality of
`r round(partition_quality(digit, fit$cluster), 3)`, compared to 69 clusters and 0.196 in the paper.
Like the paper, it splits each digit into several clusters, so the partition quality stays well
below 1.

The paper also clusters 6000 examples of the NIST digits after a random projection to 50 dimensions.
Neither the examples nor the projection are given, so this experiment cannot be repeated.

## Remaining differences

Apart from the data, `gmeans()` differs from the paper in these details:

* The test statistic is corrected for the sample size with the factor
  \(1 + 0.75/n + 2.25/n^2\) from D'Agostino and Stephens (1986), while the paper uses
  \(1 + 4/n - 25/n^2\) from Stephens (1974). At the significance level 0.0001, this gives a critical
  value of about 1.851 instead of 1.869. More importantly, the paper's factor is larger for small
  samples, so its test splits small clusters more readily: to split a cluster, the uncorrected
  statistic has to exceed about 1.64 with 20 points and 1.75 with 50 points in the paper, but 1.77
  and 1.82 here.
  Rerunning the power study with the paper's correction lowers the type II error at 50 points by
  about 0.07, which moves it further from the paper's figure, while the synthetic results barely
  change.
* Clusters with fewer than 8 points are not tested and therefore never split, since the p-value of
  the test requires at least 8 values.
* k-means uses the Hartigan-Wong algorithm, the default of `stats::kmeans()`. The paper does not
  say which algorithm it uses. With `algorithm = "Lloyd"`, `gmeans()` splits fewer Gaussian
  clusters in high dimensions: for 80 clusters in 32 dimensions, the median number of clusters found
  over 30 datasets drops from 83 to 81. Neither this nor the correction of the test statistic
  explains why the paper finds exactly 80 clusters, so the remaining gap presumably comes from
  details of the data or the implementation that the paper does not give.
